title: Palomar transients missing in Earth's shadow

tellings.quote:
said, "Yeah, you know, these objects
are falling on the dark side of the Earth
when they shouldn't be being
illuminated by the sun?"
And guess what? We get a huge deficit.
tellings.difference: Told first hand by Villarroel. She calls it a huge deficit, places it at geosynchronous distance and credits Guy Nir.
tellings.link_reason: Both tell of the Palomar transients being missing inside Earth's shadow.

as_told.title: Earth's shadow test shows a deficit of transients
as_told.place_text: Palomar plates; about 42,164 km from Earth (geosynchronous distance)

plain: Old sky photographs taken at Palomar Observatory near San Diego between 1949 and 1957 show brief points of light that appear and vanish. According to the astronomer Beatriz Villarroel, those points are strangely scarce in the part of the sky that falls in Earth's shadow. That would fit objects in orbit that flash only when sunlight hits them, before any satellites were launched. Villarroel works on this through VASCO, a project that compares old sky photographs with modern ones. She says that when her team checked a sample of these lights gathered by the Spanish Virtual Observatory, "We get a huge deficit" in the shadow. She places the effect at geosynchronous distance (the height where an orbiting object keeps pace with Earth's spin) and credits a researcher named Guy Nir. Michels later repeats her finding in another episode, describing objects that seemed absent "on the dark side of the Earth" where the sun should not light them.
